interactions.summary: Jiang pauses the reading and asks the class to summarize Beatrice's logic after the key textual claim that free will is God's greatest gift.

Jiang answers his own question by arguing that Piccarda gave her free will to God in a bond like eternal marriage, so her broken vow counts as betrayal of God rather than mere failure to keep a promise.
A student tests whether the real mistake was making the vow at all, and Jiang says yes in one sense while inviting the class to judge whether Beatrice's reasoning feels overly harsh.

claims.claim: Jiang paraphrases Beatrice's logic by saying that God's love is shown in the gift of free will, which makes the moral weight of Piccarda's vow depend on the value of that gift.
Jiang says Piccarda's decisive act was to promise her free will to God, joining the two together rather than merely promising a behavior.
Jiang intensifies the vow into an eternal marriage analogy: once Piccarda has given her free will to God, betrayal cannot be reduced to administrative vow-breaking.
Jiang states directly that what Piccarda did was not simply fail to keep a vow but betray God.
A student probes whether the underlying mistake was ever promising free will to God in the first place, exposing how radical Beatrice's account of vows is.
Jiang partially accepts the student's reformulation and immediately asks whether the class finds Beatrice's argument harsh, signaling that the extremity is intentional rather than accidental.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang recasts a vow as an eternal marriage in which free will itself becomes the pledged dowry.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is his most vivid way of explaining why Beatrice treats violated vows as betrayal rather than bookkeeping failure.

signature_moments.moment: The moral category jumps from promise-breaking to direct betrayal of God.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: That compression shows how Jiang wants the class to feel the extremity of Beatrice's logic before debating it.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Not merely a promise to do something, but the act of giving one's free will to God and entering a bond Jiang compares to eternal marriage.

chronology_notes.note: This packet is the lecture's first full paraphrase of Beatrice's textual logic: the free-will gift and vow passage is converted into Jiang's stronger betrayal model, then immediately tested by the class for harshness.
